title: Slipping away from the club; the owner turns up in New York
summary: Allen recalls the small band, how he left for St. Louis, and the owner finding him at Connie's Inn in New York.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Working the Streckfus riverboats with Fate Marable

blocks.x: All I can remember is Julio O' Toms, a piano player, but I don't remember, he was the lead, but I don't remember the rest of the nightclub. You had a plan in that? I don't remember, it was about three or four pieces. A little band. I was a small group. I used to stay in the Beans' cabin when they wanted me to knock on the wall, told me to come on and play. At that time I'd been on the boat, and I had a little pressing, I didn't play, I didn't stay there and play, just told me the water be coming out. Maybe you'll play in this, back up. I'd be in the other place, having some fun with us. So he wanted me to stay the whole winter. I got disgusted and he tells me, I'm not going to let you go back so much, you've got to stay here. And after that time I was around the Fred and I was in South. The band started at nine o'clock and the train left at seven. So I used to take my horn and he said, hey, what you taking your horn on? I said, I've got to get some lessons. He didn't want me to take my horn on at night. I used to leave it in the bar. So I started taking my horn, I made plans to leave so I took my horn off about a month straight. So one night I caught the Panama and he looked for me to open up. I would have to be at ten or eleven o'clock, I was real on the way to St. Louis saying, I gave one back and then he'd go back to the other. And the funny thing about that, I was working at Cornish Inn in 1927 and 28. Cornish Inn was a very popular band those days. And I was in a band with Adderalls and Leroy and I was sitting there playing one night and this fellow Bootsy walked in. He looked
at me and he walked up and he said, you don't know me do you? I looked at him and I said, I've seen you somewhere. He said, I'm the guy you ran away and left down the road.

He said, I'm sure you ain't seen him. I'm glad to see you very good. I'm surprised I find you in New York. I was there about two years. So he gave the band a tip and water salt and drank. He said, this guy, he said, wait for me and he took the ring. He broke the way for me. I was looking for him to come to work 19 on the train going to St. Louis. You liked St. Louis better, huh? Well at that time, I didn't catch much of St. Louis. I was raised, I was home. So I'm glad to get away. I got away and stay here. Did you play a lot of blues on that job? Played on the boat? No, in your club? Yeah, blues, most of all they played, you know, style blues and swing music, what they call it, jazz over there. But in the band on the boat we played a little everything. Complete orchestration, arrangements. And we'd ask about to make arrangements for them. It sounds very good. It's so modern and different from what they've been here. It was the same thing put together but it put together better. And the jazz and all that combined, it was quite a hit. A lot of guys come to me on and say, why don't you guys go to New York, why don't you get somewhere else, so and so and so. I guess we didn't have sense of that. That was in the very early 20s.
